newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. March output up 0.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. March output up 0.9 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. experts after the Federal Reserve said industrial production rose 0.9 percent in March compared to a revised 0.6-percent increase in February. Capacity utilization, meanwhile, rose to 84.1 percent.
Experts in a Reuters poll had expected a 0.6-percent rise in output and an 83.6-percent reading on capacity use.
KEVIN FLANAGAN, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "The numbers were stronger than expected and indicative of a manufacturing sector that continues to hum along.

"I think it is a sign of a pickup in the manufacturing sector...I think we will continue to see this buildup of inventories in manufacturing, which we had seen already in January and February numbers.

"We're going to have growth probably 2-1/2 percent to three percent in the second quarter after what looks like four percent in the first quarter ... and then I think in the second half of the year I think it will calm to something closer to two percent."

ALAN LEVENSON, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, UBS SECURITIES: "It's stronger than people expected and there's broad-based strength across the industry groups. There's also a hike in capacity utilization beyond expectations. This is a result of strong demand meeting lean inventories and producers needing to respond with strong gains in output.
"The Fed cannot be happy about the rising rates of resource utilization. Between the direction and the level (of capacity utilization) this is a reflection of the fears that the Fed has."

ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH: "It does prove what Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was worried about: that we are bumping up against capacity that could be inflationary.
"The bottom line is manufacturing has come back strongly in the first quarter of this year and it probably reflects low inventories.
"So everybody is on catch-up ... demand at the retail level and even some exports are picking up."

CHERYL KATZ, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH & CO: "Industrial production was obviously stronger than expected and concentrated in durables. But the important point in this report is we believe this strength in industrial production is not sustainable. First, we believe demand is slowing. Second, the rate of inventory building in the first quarter was extremely fast and shold slow. With inventory building slowing, that should result in slower industrial production."
On capacity use: "The fact that capacity growth is still running at over four percent should help prevent bottlenecks at the manufacturing level."
